en: Having paid homage to Jñānamūrti, the destroyer of all [wrong] views,
this classification of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) shall be explained by me out of compassion. (1)
As long as there is the conceptualization that "it exists," so long is there the conceptualization of permanence;
this is an adherence to permanence, not the true characteristic of illusion. (2)
As long as there is the conceptualization that "it does not exist," so long is there the conceptualization of annihilation.
This is an adherence to annihilation; this is not the specific characteristic of illusion.
That conceptualization which is free from existence and non-existence is the Middle Way;
this adherence to the Middle Way is not the specific characteristic of illusion. (4)
That which is called the relative truth is the characteristic of the body of the Buddhas;
this is taught as illusion, and here it is called self-consecration.
By him all this triple world, with its moving and unmoving beings, is pervaded;
he is not attained by those of little merit, but is obtained only by those who have received the prophecy.
In this [path], there is no ritual purity, no restrictive observance, no ascetic heat, and no difficult feat;
it is accomplished through non-difficult means, without observances, and with ease and joy. (7)
Having understood this, the knower of reality should repeatedly call to mind that [deity];
for him, the state of Buddhahood is accomplished through all the miraculous transformations of *māyā*. || 8 ||
O gods, yogins here always protect that which abides in illusion;
through the meditative concentration that is like an illusion, everything that is to be known indeed comes to be.
Having attained the vajra-weapon, great heroism, complete health, true happiness,
and the miraculous power of a Buddha, he travels and flies about according to his own will. (10)
And beings, impelled merely by the sight [of him], come under his control;
through the illusion-like samādhi, he obtains everything desired. (11)
Although all Buddhists declare that phenomena are like dreams and illusions, they do not realize the truth, as their minds are turned outward from their own fundamental ground. 12.

Those deluded by the analogy of an illusion do not perceive their own cognition— which is joined with wind and consciousness, which has the form of a shadow, and which is mind-made— as having the form of a shadow. 13.
Even in infinite eons, even by those who have reached the further shore of learning, *māyā* cannot be directly realized without the mouth of the Guru. (14)
Therefore, having abandoned pride and desiring the fruit of Buddhahood, one should mount the Vajrayāna and diligently propitiate the guru. || 15 ||

... having ascended [to the peak], now I shall proclaim the sequence of divisions that is very difficult to obtain; knowing which, the yogin may wander about and become composed of all the Buddhas. (16)
The four elements beginning with earth, as well as the four voids—these eight categories should be known as the causes of destruction and origination. || 17 ||
The eight categories are to be known as luminous; from that comes the great emptiness, and from that arises the means (*upāya*).
From that wisdom (*prajñā*) is produced, and from her arises the wind (*pavana*). || 18 ||
From wind arises fire, and from fire arises water; from water the earth is born—this is the origin of all beings. (19)
The element earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into the subtle element; and wind dissolves into the mind. (20)
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, but the mental factors dissolve into ignorance.
She too shall go to Prabhāsvara; this is the cessation within the three worlds.
Thus,
indeed, this wheel of existence has been revolving since beginningless time.
As long as one does not perceive the self through the illusion-like samādhi. 22.
For that illusion is self-cognizable; it is beyond the scope of logicians.
And even for the maintenance of one's own body, it is not obtained by those of meager merit. || 23 ||
[The reading *sthitā* is supported by msT; *sthitau* is the edition.
[The reading *puṇyaiḥ* is the emended edition supported by msT; *puṇyaḥ* is ms. [The reading *dṛśyate* is supported by msT; *labhyate* is the edition.]
It is known by one alone that within one's own body there exists that which is unchanging;
by the grace of the Guru's feet, it is characterized through illustrative examples. (24)
Just as treasures, jewels, and even water exist within the earth yet are not seen, so too, O All-Knowing One, [the self] exists within bodies. (25)
An illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, and Indra’s bow.
The reflection in a mirror, the moon in water, and an echo—these are [the examples]. (26)
The reflection in a mirror,
the moon in water, the surface of a dream, an illusion, a cloud, lightning, and a bubble— these are the designations [for worldly phenomena].
Illusion (māyā), which is characterized by a single nature, is explained at length through twelve similes. || 27 ||
In detail,
that which is the support of the deity regarding their state of clarity—
The threefold illusion has been pointed out; it is now being proclaimed with care. || 28 ||
The reflection in a mirror, and furthermore, the rainbow; these three are proclaimed.
One should contemplate these as the third [reflection], the moon in water, and the physical form. || 29 ||
That which has been prescribed regarding the birth [of a child], and that which is the great Buddha-family; Candra and Mūrti.
And the various deities born from each of those respective families [are also included]. (30)
Likewise, the male and female messengers, the wrathful deities, the male and female servants, and the attendants are born from those respective families.
Neither those messengers exist, nor do those female servants exist; they are manifested solely for the sake of sentient beings. (31)
The yogi should take all this away and even withdraw it into himself;
he should also cause it to expand.
The yogin, established in the illusion-like samādhi, [should perform] even the extensive [rituals] such as the maṇḍala. 32.
One should also join various kinds of syllables from the maṇḍala through self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna).
[He experiences] various kinds of sorrow, fear, detachment, terror, and likewise stumbling. || 33 ||
Discoloration, as well as agitation, mental distress, wrong views, and likewise evil deeds.
Whatever may be foul-smelling, distant, or even unpleasant to the touch;
\footnote{dūrasaṃ] \ed, durasaṃ \msT} \footnote{caiva ... cāpi] \msT, cāpi ... caiva \ed} \footnote{duḥsparśaṃ] \ed, dusparśaṃ \msT}
One should purify those various diverse natures through one's own self-mastery. || 34 ||
The natural functions such as the discharge of feces and urine, as well as diseases such as fever and the like—
Intrinsic aging and the like are their [afflictions]; for them, Māyā is the physician. || 35 ||

By which dharma the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) of fools increases upon this earth—[this is the subject of] medical treatment (*cikitsikā*). *Footnotes:* 1. *jarādyāś*: \msT\pcorr, *jvarādyāś* \msT\acorr 2. *cikitsikā*: \msT\pcorr (secunda manu), *cikittasikā* \msT\acorr, *cikitsitam* \ed.
By means of that dharma, the cycle of existence does not increase for the yogin. || 36 ||
The provisions for merit increase on this earth; the cycle of existence does not increase. The five qualities of sensual pleasure are considered by the foolish to be bonds.
By means of that dharma, the yogin should further accomplish Buddhahood. || 37 ||
Passion, joy, as well as delight, loving-kindness, and likewise compassion.
% \footnote{tathā] \ed, sp?ṣā (? \msT} % \footnote{prītir maitrī] \ed, prīti mautrīṃ \msT} % [\msT 3\verso]
Equanimity, joy, as well as strength and enthusiasm. || 38 ||
He should withdraw by means of his own presiding power the other natures (prakṛtis), whose essential forms are heroism, valor, ferocity, obstinacy, and likewise rashness. (39)
One should move about [in this manner],
either joined with a single mudrā or accompanied by four mudrās.
Or even when entered into the inner apartments, one should recollect one's own self-consecration. || 40 ||
Established in the state of great bliss, the yogi should always experience beautiful form, sound, likewise smell, taste, and touch. (41)
The stringed, the membrane-covered, the bell-like, and the wind-instrument;
||| (as well as the stretched and the expanded).
The yogi should enter the fourfold musical instruments, including the *ghana*, by means of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). 42.
One should point out all the sentiments (*rasas*), beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which are designated as the nine new dramas.
The yogi should always experience these nine arising from drama through the illusion-like samādhi. 43.
Those secret signs (*chomā*) and other extensive matters that have been fully taught in the *Yogatant*ra— [all these should be understood].
And the yogin should set those [powers] in motion through illusion (māyā), by means of non-perception. 44.
Through illusion,
whether opening or closing [the eyes], or likewise laughing or speaking, one remains without perception.
Whether speaking,
walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, one should constantly recollect the illusory body (*māyādeha*). || 45 ||
Walking,
standing, or sleeping.
Furthermore, whatever other games exist in the world, fashioned by various conceptualizations,
the knower of reality, established in the method of great passion (*mahārāga*), should engage in them as well. (46)

Having attained this self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), which shatters all views— *Note:* In the upper margin, the term *mahārāganaye* is glossed *secunda manu* as *sahaje*. It is noteworthy that the term *mahārāganaya* may have been falling out of fashion; also observe the variant *mahāsukha°* in 41d!
One may perform everything or do nothing at all, acting according to one's own pleasure. || 47 ||

One should not perform the rite of a *caitya*, nor the recitation of books; however, one may indeed perform or cause them to be recited according to the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). 48.
One should not thus pay homage to the gods, nor should one pay homage to the monks;
or else, one may pay homage to all of them according to the sequence of self-consecration.
One should not perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), nor likewise the binding of mudrās;
one should not even perform the recitation of mantras, or if one does, it should be like a mere reflection.
Whether one acts or does not act,
my mind is seen as a reflection; no external object exists.
% \footnote{bāhyamañcā] \msT\pcorr\ (secunda manu), °bāhyam atha \msT\acorr, bāhyam arthaṃ \ed} perhaps *arthaḥ* after all...
"In this way, one should indeed contemplate illusion and likewise recollect suchness. || 51 ||
By means of the rite of infinite meditation and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the mantra-form.
If illusion were not attained, [there would be no attainment] for the fruit of all the stages.
The body, enjoyments, and the environment, as well as the stages, perfections, and so forth, [are its manifestations].
The Buddha’s miraculous transformations and so forth are all the play of illusion.
Just as a form, complete with all its limbs, appears most clearly in the reflection of a mirror, so too does it appear when joined with *māyā*.
The body of Vajradhara is likewise always enriched with the eighty secondary marks and the [major] characteristics. 54.

Just as Indra’s bow, seen in the sky with its many colors, reveals the auspicious deeds of the world, so too does [the sun] reveal [the world]. *Footnote: °āḍhyo] \msT\pcorr (secunda manu) \ed, °āgro \msT\acorr.
Regarding this, \ed states that the readings were completed from the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, but it is unclear what he intends without consulting his manuscript.*
And in this way, having obtained the white and other colors in the sky, one accomplishes the ritual action in its entirety; it is indeed just like that. (55)
*vajradhṛg avāpya* (having obtained the Vajra-holder),
*varṇam*,
*sampādayati*.
And that which is situated within gold, silver, jewels, conch-shells, stones, coral, lapis lazuli, copper, silver, and so forth— [is produced] by karma; such and such [is the case].
Just as there is but one moon that appears within the expanse of the sky with a body revolving [therein], so too [is it] established in those [beginnings]. || 56 ||
Therein one [MSṬ: there itself];
for [MSṬ:
from the interior of the belly of the sky].
Thus that Lord, the Mind-Vajra, indeed exists in manifold ways among the multitude of living beings;
and he, being of universal form within his own self, consists of illusion and pervades the entire world. (57)
And the fivefold group beginning with form, as well as the sense-bases (āyatana), and indeed the eighteen elements (dhātu) that have been taught.
The five cognitions, the objects of the senses, and the entire world—all this consists of illusion; even he who is here the Vajradhara is nothing other than that. (58)
[Explicit: \msT] Just as Vajradhṛk,
so too are all the mountains, the eight great oceans, the continents, and the various divisions of the hells and so forth.
Whatever is seen, whether stationary or moving, that is itself the omniscient one alone, and nothing else. 59.

Thus, having realized that this entire world is nothing but one's own mind, those who are liberated from the conceptualization of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and who do not wander in the great oceans of worldly construction—homage be to them, who have reached the further shore of all conditioned things. (60)
The *Svādhiṣṭhānaprabheda* is completed. This work is by the venerable Āryadeva.
